pages.title: Start here: how the channel runs

text.text: One video a week, one or two Shorts, and every sponsor read on time. This page explains where each piece lives and the order the team works in.
The weekly rhythm
Monday:
the host and producer pick the next shoot from the Idea column of Videos and write the promise for each one.
Shoot day:
everything filmed that day links to its row in Shoot days, so the planned minutes add up and the producer can see if the day is overbooked.
Editing:
the editor moves the video to Editing and then Packaging once the cut is locked. Packaging means title, thumbnail, chapters and description, nothing else.
Upload:
set the Publish date, upload as scheduled, and press
Mark published
the day it goes live. That stamps the real date, which can differ from the plan.
Day 28:
fill in views, click-through rate, average viewed and ad revenue from the channel analytics. RPM and the Packaging check fill themselves.
Who owns what
Rules that keep the channel healthy
A video without a promise sentence does not get a shoot day.
Shorts come from footage already shot for a long video; they never get their own shoot.
A sponsor is linked to a video only once the contract is signed, so the Effective CPM reads true.
What the channel needs from you this week: videos past their publish date, sponsor drafts coming due, and money still owed by brands. Views and RPM are from each video's first 28 days.

pages.title: Packaging a video: title, thumbnail, first 30 seconds

text.text: Packaging is the step between a locked cut and the upload. A strong video with weak packaging dies in the first two days, because nobody clicks it. Give it its own stage on the board and its own owner.
Start from the promise

Every video row has a promise sentence in its plan. The title and the thumbnail are two different ways of saying that promise, and they must not repeat each other. If the title says what was built, the thumbnail shows the surprising part: the crack in the slab, the price tag, the before and after.
Titles
Write three titles before anyone opens the thumbnail file. One plain, one with a number or a cost, one with a question.
Keep the meaning in the first 45 characters; phones cut the rest.
Never promise something the video does not show in the first two minutes. Viewers leave, and average viewed drops.
Thumbnails
One subject, readable at the size of a postage stamp. Check it on a phone, not the editing monitor.
Three words at most on the image, and never the same words as the title.
The designer mocks up two versions; the host picks one and ticks
Thumbnail approved
. Nothing moves to Scheduled without that tick.
The first 30 seconds

Open on the finished piece or the problem, then say what the viewer will get. Channel name, sponsor read and shop tour all come later. The sponsor read sits after the first build step, never in the opening.
Reading the results at day 28

cells.text: Reuse the thumbnail style for the series
Try a second thumbnail on the next upload in the series
Change the title and thumbnail now; older videos can recover

text.text: Shorts and live streams skip the check, because their views come from the feed, not from a click on a thumbnail. Look at RPM beside it: a tool test with a lower click rate but a high RPM can still be the better video for the business.
Worked example

The budget track saw test went out with the title in plain words and a thumbnail showing the price tag beside a perfect cut. It clicked at 8.1%, the best of the quarter, so the next tool test copies that layout: object, price, proof.

pages.title: Sponsor reads, from pitch to payment

text.text: Sponsor money keeps the shop running between ad payouts, but one bad read costs more trust than it earns. This is how the partnerships manager takes a deal from first email to paid.
1. Pitched and Negotiating

Every brand that writes in or that we approach gets a row in Sponsors with the Brand sponsor brief filled in. The first question is always whether we would use the product in the shop if nobody paid us. If not, mark it Declined and say so politely.
During negotiation, settle four things and write them on the row: the
Deliverable
(an integrated read, a dedicated video or a short mention), the
Fee
, the
Usage rights
(whether the brand may run our clip as a paid ad and for how long) and
Category exclusivity
. Paid usage and exclusivity are worth extra; price them separately rather than giving them away.
2. Contracted and Script review
Once the contract is signed, press
New sponsored video
on the sponsor row. It opens a video plan already linked to the brand.
Set the
Script draft due
date. Most brands want the read script about a week before filming.
Send the read, not the whole video script. Brands approve their 60 seconds; they never approve our opinions about their competitors.
3. Live and Invoiced

When the video goes live, the sponsor moves to Live. Send the invoice with the live link the same day and move it to Invoiced. The Awaiting payment view on the dashboard shows every brand in Live or Invoiced, so nothing waits quietly for 60 days.
4. Paid
Press
Mark paid
when the money lands. It stamps the date, which shows which brands pay on time when it is renewal season.
Is a deal worth it?
The
Effective CPM
divides the fee by the views the sponsored videos earned in their first 28 days, times a thousand. Compare it with the channel's ad RPM:

cells.text: Underpriced; ask for more on renewal
A fair deal for a woodworking audience
A strong partner; offer them first refusal on the next series

text.text: A dedicated video usually shows a lower CPM than a read, because the whole video is theirs; price it at two to three times a read.
The upload plan for the next eight weeks, with every video placed on its publish date and the pipeline beside it. A gap on the calendar is a gap in the channel.
Shoot days ahead
A shoot day is the most expensive day of the month. Batch two or three videos per day, plan the shot list the week before, and wrap with every card backed up twice.
The week before
Every video on the day has a finished script or a beat sheet, and is linked to the shoot day.
Write the shot list per video: the A-roll talking parts, the B-roll close-ups, and the one hero shot for the thumbnail.
Build materials and tools are bought and on the bench. A missing part stops a shop build cold.
Order of the day
Light and sound check first, 20 minutes, with a test clip played back on a laptop, not the camera screen.
Shoot the thumbnail hero shot while the set is clean.
A-roll for every video while your energy is up; B-roll after lunch.
Slate every take with the video's title; the editor will thank you.
Shorts last: pull two vertical moments from the day's best work.
Wrap
Cards copied to the editing drive and to the backup drive before they are formatted
Footage folder named with the shoot date and video titles
Shoot day marked Wrapped; videos moved to Editing
Receipts for materials attached to the shoot day's page
Planning numbers
If the edit queue is more than two weeks long, skip the next shoot and help the editor catch up. Footage nobody can publish is not a buffer.
